description: FIRST Cyber Threat Intelligence Symposium talks from FIRST Cyber Threat Intelligence Symposium 2022.

talks.title: FIRST SIG Updates
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in FIRST SIG Updates.
talks.summary:
Overview: FIRST SIG leaders present updates at the Cyber Threat Intelligence Symposium, covering CVSS v4.0 development and other special interest group progress.

Key Topics: CVSS v4.0 finer granularity metrics and attack requirements; 3,000 person-hours of SIG effort; BTE (Base, Threat, Environmental) scoring model; public preview targeting December 2022; and other FIRST SIG initiatives.

Technical Details: Dave Dugal presents CVSS v4.0 improvements including enhanced user interaction metrics, attack requirements, and a bit.ly calculator preview for community feedback before NIST math finalization.

Takeaways: CVSS v4.0 addresses long-standing scoring granularity complaints. Security teams should review the preview calculator and provide feedback to shape the final specification.

talks.title: 0-day In-the-Wild Exploitation in 2022...so far.
talks.teaser: Examines the zero-day exploits seen actively exploited in the wild during 2022 and why many are variants of patched bugs.
talks.summary:
Project Zero’s Zero-Day Mission

Google Project Zero researcher Maddie Stone tracks zero-days exploited in the wild to drive structural mitigations and “make zero-day hard”—raising exploit cost and requiring more bugs per capability. She maintains public spreadsheets and a GitHub repository of in-the-wild zero-days since mid-2014.

2022 Statistics So Far

Through 2022 the team counted 18 in-the-wild zero-days. Nine were variants of previously patched bugs; four were variants of 2021 zero-days attackers reused within roughly twelve months because patches were incomplete. Stone argues this shows zero-days are not yet “hard.”

What “Hard” Would Look Like

Remote phone compromise via a link still typically chains about three zero-days (renderer RCE, sandbox escape, local privilege escalation). Harder ecosystems would require more chained bugs, novel bug classes, undocumented attack surfaces, non-reusable exploit techniques, and highly selective deployment rather than broad watering-hole burns.

talks.title: A Diamond is an Analysts Best Friend Introducing the Diamond Model for Influence Operations Analysis
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of A Diamond is an Analysts Best Friend Introducing the Diamond Model for Influence Operations Analysis.
talks.summary:
Defining Influence Operations

Recorded Future analyst Charity Wright opens a TLP:WHITE session distinguishing misinformation, disinformation, and fake news. Influence operations are organized attempts to change target-audience beliefs and decisions, often through propaganda and mass manipulation rather than kinetic effects alone.

Limits of Existing Frameworks

Prior analysis focused on content, voice, and dissemination but missed relationships among narratives, actors, and infrastructure. Kill chains like MITRE's disinformation chain and the AMITT TTP catalog help map adversary process yet lack psychosocial and geopolitical nuance, and new platforms outpace static TTP lists.

Narrative as the Core

Wright stresses that every campaign centers on a story. Humans assign meaning through narrative, especially stories invoking shared identity. Narrative warfare weaponizes those meanings to change behavior, an element often lost in technically focused CTI tradecraft.

The Adapted Diamond Model

Building on the 2013 intrusion Diamond Model, Wright's influence variant places narrative at the center. Technical axes retain capabilities and infrastructure; socio-political axes rename adversary to influencer and victim to audience, fusing essential campaign components for daily analysis of complex psychosocial threats.

talks.title: Attack Flow
talks.teaser: Beyond Atomic Behaviors examines Attack Flow.
talks.summary:
Beyond atomic behaviors

MITRE's Desiree Beck, Verizon's Gabriel Bassett, and Fujitsu's Ryu Masuka present Attack Flow, a Center for Threat-Informed Defense project. They argue CTI and incident response suffer when analysts treat isolated indicators as noise instead of recognizing related steps as a meaningful campaign sequence.

What an attack flow is

An attack flow models coordinated adversary behavior as structured objects and relationships rather than disconnected atomic events. Poor sequence understanding leads to weaker containment and remediation when campaigns unfold across multiple stages.

Graph representation with RDF

The data model builds on RDF triples—subject, predicate, object—mapped to source, relationship, and destination. This graph foundation supports reasoning across linked techniques, assets, and actions, with tooling aligned to semantic web standards for sharing and analysis at scale.

talks.title: Being A Better Defender By Channeling Your Worst Adversary:
talks.teaser: Shows how a defender can build adversary emulations from threat reports to find detection blind spots.
talks.summary:
John Stoner, presenting for Cisco, explains how his team used adversary emulation mainly to find detection blind spots in their enterprise, so that repeated hunts could become alerts for operations teams. The work began with a single nation-state style actor, using spearphishing and PowerShell Empire modules, with Linux visibility added through osquery and cloud logging checked across AWS, Azure, GCP and Microsoft 365.

Later he built a new scenario from a public Microsoft report chain: a phishing email, a link file opening a PDF, PowerShell and a Cobalt Strike download. Because that tool was not available to his team, they substituted Metasploit, moved from Windows 7 to Windows 10, and added Azure AD synchronization. Each step was mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques with command lines and timestamps, and validation runs revealed missing events, sometimes exposing misconfigurations. As remote work and newer threat reporting shaped the emulation, they added script block logging, SQL auditing in the cloud, and ADFS golden SAML and Graph API MFA bypass scenarios.

Stoner's lessons: keep scenarios realistic rather than perfect, aim to reproduce the outcome rather than every variant, and bound the scope to what the team can absorb. Expect things to break, treat prevention blocks as useful signals, and store datasets so they can be replayed with curveballs. Representative personas, always-on infrastructure, and watching for diminishing returns on time spent round out the advice. Focus on goals, attack sequences, and logging gaps.

talks.title: Beyond Incident Reporting - An Analysis of Structured Representations for Incident Response
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Beyond Incident Reporting - An Analysis of Structured Representations for Incident Response.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Presented by Marco Caselli (Siemens) and Daniel Schlette (University of Regensburg), this presentation explores how organizations can represent, evaluate, and operationalize incident response (IR) procedures beyond basic Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) indicators. Drawing on research from the European project Concordia and standards development (including OASIS CACAO and OpenC2), the speakers analyze existing structured formats for IR playbooks and examine the organizational factors required to adapt shared playbooks to specific enterprise environments.

### Key Topics
- **Evolution from CTI to IR Courses of Action**: Shifting from atomic indicators of compromise (hashes, IP addresses) and TTPs toward standardized courses of action and executable playbooks.
- **Categorization of IR Standards**: Distinguishing between high-level frameworks (e.g., RE&CT, MITRE D3FEND), procedural playbook formats (e.g., CACAO), and granular command-level execution standards (e.g., OpenC2).
- **Core Structural and Evaluation Concepts**: Breaking IR down to essential structural primitives—workflow, actuator, action, and artifact—and evaluating standards against general, technological, and security criteria.
- **Organizational Factors and Context**: Examining why technical representations alone are insufficient for cross-organization sharing due to variations in legal regulations, internal policies, team resources, and command structures.

### Technical Details
At its base, incident response consists of a workflow where an actuator executes an action on an artifact. While an analysis of existing standards revealed that all formats adequately cover the core *actions*, coverage of actuators, workflows, and artifacts varies significantly. 

To evaluate formats for specific use cases (such as playbook sharing, automation, and internal management reporting), the speakers derived broader evaluation criteria:
- **General Concepts**: Aggregability (bundling IR steps together), versioning, and machine vs. human readability.
- **Technology Concepts**: Community backing, serialization formats, and implementation scope.
- **Security Concepts**: Confidentiality markings (e.g., TLP, IEP), authorization requirements prior to execution, and prioritization.

Applying these criteria to an incident response sharing use case, CACAO emerged as a strong candidate because it structures procedures into workflows and steps, aggregates playbook information, is backed by an OASIS community, and supports confidentiality markings (TLP/IEP). However, technical playbooks must be contextualized using an organization's specific operational factors. The authors proposed conceptualizing a transformation engine that merges technical playbooks with organizational context to automatically tailor response steps. Key organizational dimensions include:
1. **External Regulations & Compliance**: E.g., GDPR requiring legal consultation before analyzing customer data.
2. **Internal Policies**: E.g., rules requiring IP redirection rather than direct blocking, or restrictions on copying forensic files.
3. **Attacker Context & Responsibility**: E.g., past encounters with a threat group triggering escalation branches to the CISO.
4. **Security Setting & Resources**: Team size, budget, tooling, and time limits.

### Takeaways
Standardized formats like CACAO provide structured, machine-readable mechanisms to represent IR procedures, but technical playbooks cannot simply be imported without accounting for an organization's specific context. Ongoing research and industry feedback aim to formally categorize organizational factors so that automated transformation engines can adapt shared community playbooks to local constraints, compliance rules, and technical architectures.

talks.title: Bridging Together Independent Islands - STIX Custom Objects and Matching Mechanisms to Correlate...
talks.teaser: Shows how custom STIX objects and fuzzy matching can link Japanese and English name records in threat intelligence data.
talks.summary:
The talk begins with a Japanese law enforcement case in which criminal records held identifiers such as IP addresses and bank accounts, all of which needed correlating. The speakers first assumed STIX custom objects would solve it, but personal names broke that idea. A Japanese bank form asked for name fields in kanji and katakana, and sometimes hiragana, while a US account needed only given, middle and family names.

Transliteration added another layer. A katakana given name can be romanized in several ways, and a passport spelling may not match the others, while some Russian family names vary by gender. The speakers extended their SHIP platform with three features: a GUI for modeling custom objects and properties, explicit correlation rules that restrict which fields are compared, and fuzzy matching that covers letter case, kana variants, synonym lists and alternate spellings. In the demo, a katakana name was linked to an English person object through a fuzzy match shown in a graph view.

The main takeaway is that cross-language matching needs configurable rules rather than a single fixed standard, and the speakers described it as partly an art. Planned work includes applying the approach to real investigations, speeding up matching, handling other notations and structural differences, and sharing object schemas and matching rules.

talks.title: Build Automated Malware Lab with CERT.pl Open-Source Software
talks.teaser: Walks through CERT.pl's open-source malware lab for collecting, analysing and sharing samples and configurations.
talks.summary:
The talk presents an open-source malware analysis lab built by CERT.pl, the Polish national CERT team within the NASK research institute. The team works as a threat intelligence operation, and malware is the second largest source of incidents in its constituency. Their goals are to spot campaigns early, warn victims and mitigate threats. Their tooling grew from case-by-case scripts into a generic framework as commodity banking trojans spread.

The lab rests on three roles: collecting samples, plugging in family-specific analysis and sharing results. MWDB stores files, configurations and blobs for analysts, and Karton is a Redis-based microservice framework where small single-purpose scripts, such as a file classifier or an archive extractor, chain into pipelines. A public portal offers access to samples and analyser outputs, with over 1,000 accounts and analysers for roughly 130 families, many of which are no longer maintained.

The final section covered similarity analysis as a plugin. Windows API usage taken from sandbox memory dumps becomes a feature vector shown in a results tab, which helps classify variants that existing YARA rules miss. The presenters noted that fuzzy matching is not guaranteed to be meaningful, and a planned extension compares normalised disassembled functions across their dataset. Documentation, training materials and a command-line interface were pointed out for anyone wanting to build a similar lab.

talks.title: CERT-UA: Research and Technical Analysis of Large-Scale Cyber Attacks in Ukraine in 2021
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for CERT-UA: Research and Technical Analysis of Large-Scale Cyber Attacks in Ukraine in 2021.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Presented at FIRSTcon in Dublin, representatives from Ukraine’s State Service of Special Communication and Information Protection (SSSCIP) and CERT-UA shared operational insights into large-scale cyber warfare targeting Ukraine in 2022. While originally scheduled to cover 2021, the speakers pivoted to cover real-time technical analysis of cyberattacks unfolding during the Russian invasion, detailing wiper campaigns, defacements, DDoS attacks, supply-chain compromises, and phishing operations.

### Key Topics
- **Incident Volume and Targeted Sectors:** CERT-UA registered 1,306 incidents by the time of the presentation, with roughly half classified as critical or high severity. The government sector was the primary target, followed by military organizations, financial institutions, commercial entities, energy, telecoms, and IT.
- **January 14 Supply-Chain Attacks:** A major coordinated attack defaced and wiped dozens of government web servers via a compromised IT service provider that developed sites for multiple state agencies.
- **Pre-Invasion Destructive Operations:** In the hours preceding the February 24 physical invasion, massive coordinated wiper deployments and DDoS attacks struck Ukrainian banks, government infrastructure, and media outlets.
- **Threat Actor Activities:** Analysis of prominent threat groups targeting Ukraine, including Sandworm (destructive wipers), Gamaredon/Armageddon (phishing and espionage), APT29, and hacktivist-style groups like the "Cyber Army of Russia Reborn" (UAC-0107).

### Technical Details
- **January 14 Attack Mechanics:** Although initial hypotheses pointed to an October CMS vulnerability, log analysis revealed threat actors manually accessed servers via SSH, established persistence with new user accounts, and removed `index.php` by hand. Concurrently, endpoints suffered destructive wiping via `stage1.exe` (identified by Microsoft as WhisperGate / BootPatch), executed through Impacket from compromised web servers. In several environments, actors logged directly into hypervisors and destroyed virtual machine configurations.
- **Sandworm Wiper Playbook:** In nearly 99% of wiper incidents analyzed across roughly 15 organizations, Sandworm bypassed phishing entirely in favor of exploiting public-facing web applications, Microsoft Exchange servers, and VPNs (including instances where two-factor authentication had been disabled). For post-exploitation, attackers created SSH tunnels and proxy networks using Stowaway, alongside Impacket for lateral movement and command execution.
- **Specialized Malware & ICS Targeting:** In an attack on a Ukrainian power plant, responders recovered CaddyWiper variants and Industroyer2, accompanied by custom wipers specifically engineered for Solaris, Linux, and industrial control systems.
- **Phishing Tactics & Tooling:** Gamaredon frequently registered `.site` top-level domains (e.g., matching keywords like `military-ukraine` or `gov-ua`) and abused legitimate infrastructure such as Wix and Zimbra vulnerabilities (which allowed attackers to harvest hundreds of emails or inject malicious JavaScript to forward victim messages). In some campaigns, threat actors impersonated CERT-UA or abused CERT-UA's IP addresses by routing C2 traffic to cert.gov.ua to trigger global ISP blacklisting.

### Takeaways
- **Cyber as a Domain of War:** Modern hybrid warfare tightly integrates pre-conflict and wartime cyber strikes with kinetic operations, targeting government continuity, civilian morale, and critical infrastructure.
- **Process & Operational Resilience:** Under wartime conditions, CERT-UA and SSSCIP re-engineered operations, relocated personnel to ensure safety, and shifted to secure remote workflows.
- **Global Collaboration:** Effective response and attribution rely heavily on real-time data sharing and technical support from international CERTs, cybersecurity vendors, independent researchers, and commercial IT partners.

talks.title: Community Management and Tool Orchestration the Open-Source Way via Cerebrate
talks.teaser: Shows how Cerebrate centralises contacts, sharing groups and MISP fleet management for security communities.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Cerebrate, an open-source tool built by a Luxembourg-based team that also develops MISP. The speakers explain the problems that grow with large information-sharing communities: trust between members, identity management for many organisations, and sharing groups that each party has to recreate by hand. They also describe the contact data a community needs to keep, from organisation details and sector to IP ranges, AS numbers and cryptographic keys used for signing.

Cerebrate is presented as a central contact database holding organisations, individuals, sharing groups, distribution lists and keys. Organisation records are shaped by JSON metadata templates, so a community can add fields such as CIDR blocks or AS numbers, with type-aware search on those fields. The speakers describe an API documented with OpenAPI, Keycloak integration so that community members can manage their own teams with limited rights, and public indexes that other tools can query. A demo shows a MISP connector that manages several MISP instances from one place, and an integration layer where a three-way handshake handles interconnection requests between nodes.

Planned work includes trusted synchronisation connections that can update existing data, full data signing in MISP, and more tool integrations. The takeaway is that one authoritative node can handle contacts, sharing groups and tool connections for a community, and that the integration layer is designed so others can add their own tools.

talks.title: Creating an Information Security/Information Assurance Program
talks.teaser: Shares lessons from a federal health research agency on building an information security program that serves its mission.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who has spent about 25 years in US federal information security and built programs at several organizations, opens with a central point: a security program has to be framed as an enabler of the organization's mission, not as a blocker. He advises first working out where his own jurisdiction sits within a larger body, and who the customers and stakeholders are, including internal leadership, contractors and information-sharing groups, because internal politics shape what gets prioritized.

On the team side, he distinguishes formal staff from virtual or ad hoc help and walks through core functions such as vulnerability and configuration management, incident response, privacy, legal, human resources and communications, noting that one person may cover several of them. He also maps the regulatory obligations that apply across jurisdictions and identifies dependencies on help desk, server and network teams, plus outside providers. Bringing digital forensics in-house is presented as a key step that reduced reliance on others.

For proactive work, he describes audits as snapshots in time and favors ongoing authorization, timely vulnerability fixes, penetration testing and threat intelligence. He accepts that reactive incident response will always be needed and that faster detection limits damage. In the question period he said legal involvement depends on how an organization is structured, and he described securing public-facing systems during the pandemic.

talks.title: CSAF - the Magic Potion for Vulnerability Handling in Industrial Environments
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in CSAF - the Magic Potion for Vulnerability Handling in Industrial Environments.

talks.title: CSIRT and SOC Modernization Practices
talks.teaser: Explains how incident response teams can plan, measure and redesign their services, roles and processes using maturity models.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how CSIRTs and SOCs can move beyond day-to-day operations and deliberately improve themselves. The speaker describes modernization as a cycle: operate, review annual performance against stakeholder expectations, choose a limited set of initiatives within the approved budget and resources, then design and implement them. A common first step is to clarify the mandate, stating what the team does and does not do, because unclear responsibilities confuse stakeholders and weaken trust.

The speaker then walks through how a change should cascade. Services lead to processes and workflows, which shape the organization, skills and training, facilities, technology and, finally, communication with partners such as law enforcement, other agencies and the media. For assessment, the talk points to two maturity models: SOC-CMM, which is very detailed, and the lighter SIM3. It also covers the FIRST services framework mapped to roughly 26 to 27 roles, along with NIST NICE and ENISA role work for defining skills. Teams should pick services that fit their own context rather than copy others, and monitoring is treated as a service that is not always present at national or sectoral level.

For measurement, the speaker gives examples of monthly metrics. The number of open incidents at month end should normally be above zero, a growing backlog of unclosed incidents is a warning sign, and SLA breaches should be tracked. Metrics that do not inform decisions should be dropped. Team size guides which maturity target is realistic, with larger teams suited to SOC-CMM and teams of seven to fifteen people often aiming at SIM3. The main takeaways are to define a clear purpose, check the mandate, measure only what will be used, and publicly recognize improvements.

talks.title: Cyber Ireland - Addressing Cyber Crime Through Industry-Academia-Government Collaboration
talks.teaser: Describes how Ireland measures its cybersecurity sector and coordinates industry, academia, and government through a national cluster model.
talks.summary:
Owen Byrne outlines Cyber Ireland, the national industry cluster established in 2018 to give Ireland’s fragmented cybersecurity companies a shared voice. He argues that national resilience depends as much on economic, political, and workforce factors as on technical controls, and that no single agency can solve those problems alone.

He presents findings from a recent sector sizing exercise: roughly 7,500 people across about 490 firms, split between pure-play security vendors and diversified multinationals with SOCs or product-security teams, with strong hubs in Dublin, Cork, Galway, and Limerick. Revenue and employment trends point toward significant growth by 2030, but surveys highlight skills gaps, financing constraints, small domestic company scale, and weak industry–academia R&D collaboration. Byrne ties these gaps to high cybercrime costs, weak formal security strategies among businesses, the HSE ransomware incident, and a mismatch between Ireland’s digital economy strength and comparatively low cybersecurity preparedness.

The second half details how the cluster operationalizes collaboration: regional workshops, a multi-stakeholder advisory board, community building, talent pathways with universities, research matchmaking, export and investor events, diversity initiatives, youth camps, and a volunteer expert panel that supported healthcare during a major incident. He closes by contrasting cooperation with shared long-term collaboration aimed at national resilience, and fielded questions on schools outreach, sector mapping methods, government funding pitches, and graduate readiness.

talks.title: Cybersecurity Maturity in the Pacific Islands - Integrating CERT Services in a Regional Framework
talks.teaser: Explores a conceptual model for aligning national CERT services across Pacific Island nations within a shared regional framework.
talks.summary:
Pacific Island countries are at an early stage of building cybersecurity self-reliance. Collaboration between nations is largely organic, and a previous regional CERT effort is no longer active. Adams frames the gap as heightened vulnerability and a drag on investment for governments, residents, businesses, and outside partners across the region.

The research aims to produce a theoretical model and a practical toolkit so interventions and capability maturity work can target the highest‑return priorities instead of one-size-fits-all programs. The proposed framework rests on affiliated national CERTs that align capabilities to domestic priorities first, then collaborate where interests overlap, with universities, NGOs, and bodies such as FIRST or the ITU supporting governed, planned assistance. National, regional, and global drivers link through governance, aligned CERTs, and a central focus on which services each country runs locally versus shares. Cultural-historical activity theory is used to capture tensions among governments, CERT services, and regional engagement as opportunities to grow the shared middle.

An initial validation study with participants worldwide found broad resonance. Common service interests included threat detection, incident response, forensics, and advisory work, plus community awareness. Trust, people over technology, and respect for national priorities emerged as cross-cutting themes. Upcoming case studies will test the model across Polynesia, Micronesia, Melanesia, and a small island state, with capability maturity called out as the dominant national need still lacking clear answers.

talks.title: Decoding the Diversity Discussion
talks.teaser: Links diversity and inclusion themes to practical incident response habits across preparation, detection, containment, and recovery.
talks.summary:
The speaker compares how security teams learned to demand actionable threat intelligence with how diversity and inclusion conversations often stop at strategy without clear individual or team actions. She argues that varied perspectives strengthen incident response, but everyday response work still leaves people out through language, process design, and crisis pressure.

The talk walks the incident response lifecycle with concrete inclusion points. Preparation covers reframing training labels, supplementing long playbooks with checklists and visuals, and making tabletop exercises safe for quieter participants. Detection and analysis emphasize responder welfare, brief introductions during stand-ups, and pre-tested out-of-band channels so remote or new members are not added hours late. Containment and recovery address discussing disruptive measures without shutting down unfamiliar voices, replacing exclusionary security terminology, and writing executive briefings for non-specialists. Post-incident work balances lessons learned with mental health support, anonymous feedback options, and documenting successes as well as gaps. She also notes platform features for time zones, pronouns, and accessibility.

The closing mantra is to assume less and ask more so people seek clarity comfortably under pressure. Audience questions extend this to listening through blind spots, drawing input from timid experts when managers dominate, and proactive introductions that humanize roles across legal, HR, communications, and technical functions.

talks.title: DNS as Added Security Against Ransomware Attacks
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for DNS as Added Security Against Ransomware Attacks.

talks.title: Don't Blame the User! Stop the Phish Before it is Even Sent
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Don't Blame the User! Stop the Phish Before it is Even Sent.

talks.title: EDR Internals From a Defenders Perspective
talks.teaser: Explains how Microsoft Defender for Endpoint collects telemetry, where its blind spots are, and how to tune it.
talks.summary:
Olaf Hartung, a defensive specialist at FalconForce, looks at what Microsoft Defender for Endpoint actually does on a Windows host. He walks through its parts: antivirus that relies mainly on signatures with some cloud analysis, attack surface reduction rules, application control, and the EDR sensor. The sensor ships events to a cloud store for advanced hunting, where data is kept for about 30 days. Microsoft decides which events are logged, and some sources such as network connections are heavily rate limited, so beaconing is hard to see from this data.

He then explains how the telemetry is gathered. The product uses kernel callbacks and Event Tracing for Windows, with its own aggregation providers and a local store that forwards events when connectivity drops. The collection is driven by a signed configuration that sets event filters, global and local caps, and dynamic data collection scripts. Some events, such as service creation and scheduled tasks, only appear if specific Windows audit policies are enabled, and the speaker found that Microsoft does not document which of these it enables. He also noted that the diagnostics tracing service could be stopped or paused by a local administrator, which would suspend parts of the telemetry stream.

For practitioners, the main takeaway is to verify what the product actually sees in their own environment. Check audit policies in group policy, because local settings can override the ones the product expects. Review exclusions and attack surface reduction rules, since both can be abused, and consider application control in audit mode and native event logs to fill gaps. Hartung closes by arguing that vendors should document their telemetry coverage so defenders can understand where the product is strong and where it needs supplementing.

talks.title: Endorsing the New Rules
talks.teaser: Traces how UN cyber norms were negotiated and why incident responders are asked to support them.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who has spent about 25 years in security work, recounts serving as the only non-diplomat in a 15-member United Nations group of governmental experts on cyber norms. Since 2004 six such groups have met, and four reached consensus reports that the General Assembly endorsed. The reports are non-binding, but they include a set of 11 norms of responsible state behaviour from 2015 that apply to everyone and offer a starting point for practitioners.

The middle of the talk covers the open-ended working group, which is open to NGOs and the private sector, and the role the texts assign to CERTs and incident responders in cooperation and confidence-building. The speaker argues that trust has to be built before a crisis, that multi-stakeholder partnership is essential to implementation, and that CERTs should not be turned into offensive tools or politicised. Attribution is presented as difficult because of proxies and anonymised traffic.

In the question session, an attendee from an EU public administration described how CERTs supply evidence on which diplomatic attribution decisions rest, and the speaker answered that CERTs should keep distance from law enforcement and political debate. A later question about protecting a national CERT from politicisation drew the reply that a position distant from political decisions makes a CERT more effective. The closing message is that practitioners should learn the norms, involve legal experts, and engage with the UN processes.

talks.title: Enhancing Operations Through the Tracking of Interactive Linux-based Intrusion Campaigns
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Enhancing Operations Through the Tracking of Interactive Linux-based Intrusion Campaigns.

talks.title: Follow the Dynamite: Commemorating TeamTNT's Cloud Attacks
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Follow the Dynamite: Commemorating TeamTNT's Cloud Attacks.

talks.title: Formulating An Intelligence-Driven Threat Hunting Methodology
talks.teaser: Lays out a repeatable threat hunting process that links adversary behavior, available visibility and business risk to detection.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the idea that threat hunting is a proactive search for intrusions that earlier controls missed, and argues that it should be a repeatable process rather than an ad hoc exercise. The speaker proposes three inputs: an understanding of how relevant adversaries operate, a clear view of the telemetry the organization actually has (host, network and file or artifact data), and an understanding of which assets and risks matter most. Hunting hypotheses built from these inputs should be specific, measurable, detectable, timely and testable, so that a hunt can be evaluated and refined.

The middle of the talk works through two examples. For business email compromise, the hunt looks for spoofed or injected messages through email header anomalies and missing DKIM signatures, tied to the financial loss the attacker is after. For a ransomware intrusion, the speaker describes a reported case that moved from phishing and initial access to ransomware deployment in about three and a half hours, using Cobalt Strike, PsExec, WMI, AdFind, BloodHound and domain controller compromise. A hunt aimed at the early discovery phase would look for unusual Active Directory enumeration, such as high volumes of LDAP queries. The speaker also touches on credential abuse, suggesting checks for one-to-many remote logon patterns and attempts to bypass multi-factor authentication, and notes that cloud hunting remains a difficult, provider-specific problem.

The closing point is that a hunt which must be repeated should become an automated detection. The speaker describes a cycle in which the detection baseline is established first, hunts cover gaps beyond it, and validated hunts are then automated, steadily improving coverage over time.

talks.title: Global IR in a Fragmented World
talks.teaser: Examines how UN cyber norms and state espionage collaterally affect CSIRTs defending users across a borderless internet.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens with the tension when vendors patch flaws tied to their own government’s operations, then walks through decades of public state-sponsored activity to argue that espionage—not “cyber war”—dominates, often with outsized harm once exploits leak to criminals.

He contrasts physical and online constraints: weakened territorial sovereignty, difficult attribution, one-to-many “class breaks,” rapid innovation, asymmetry, and the absence of a global enforcer. He surveys UN Group of Governmental Experts milestones, the Open-Ended Working Group, parallel cybercrime talks, and initiatives such as the Paris Call, treating norms as voluntary behavior that may harden into custom. Highlighted norms shield incident response teams from attack and politicization, while vulnerability cases—from Microsoft Exchange through Log4j and national equity processes—show how disclosure rules hit industry. Switzerland’s Geneva Dialogue and national stances on stockpiling illustrate uneven clarity.

FIRST’s stated goals include keeping responder tools lawful, enabling cross-border cooperation despite sanctions, prioritizing user safety over intelligence convenience, protecting core infrastructure, and building communities—not only training. Practitioners should avoid attribution politics, lean on ethics guidance for disclosure dilemmas, and engage policymakers. Q&A extends sovereignty questions to multinational cloud data and whether routing or cable interception belongs in the same “core internet” conversation.

talks.title: Going with the (work)flow? Incident Response for Vicious Workflows
talks.teaser: Shows how exposed Argo and Airflow workflow dashboards leak credentials, and how to check and protect your own.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at open-source workflow platforms, which let teams chain tasks into scheduled pipelines, and asks whether their exposed dashboards can be found and what they reveal without exploiting any bug. The speakers focused on two projects. Argo Workflows is a container-native engine built for Kubernetes, where the server mode gives anyone who can reach it the permissions of its deployment. Researchers located internet-facing instances through scan datasets, certificate and DNS lookups, and brute-forced subdomain guesses. In one cluster they found a Monero miner that had been running for eight months.

The Airflow case was the more alarming. Exposed dashboards showed hardcoded API keys in task code and secrets kept as plain variables. Connection credentials were often placed in the unencrypted extra field instead of the password field. Older versions logged credentials typed into the CLI in plain text, a configuration view could be displayed when a flag was enabled, and an ad hoc query feature let anyone reach connected databases without authentication. A swapped container image or the code editor plugin could also run a crypto miner, which the team demonstrated in a test lab.

The takeaway was that single weaknesses become serious when chained: an open firewall, missing authentication, hardcoded secrets and over-privileged cloud keys. Practitioners should avoid quickstart defaults in production, apply least privilege, patch promptly and plan for layered defenses. The speakers also pointed to git-secrets for blocking committed secrets, Custodian for enforcing cloud policy, and Magpie for discovering what is exposed.

talks.title: How I Handled One of the Biggest Banking Fraud Incidents of 2020
talks.teaser: A SOC walks through a 2020 Brazil banking fraud case where fake sites showed live account data piped from real bank APIs.
talks.summary:
The session opens with Brazil’s fraud landscape around PIX: enormous daily transfer volume and street-level coercion, then shifts to a Christmas 2020 case at an NTT-managed SOC. A customer report of a fake banking URL led analysts to something worse than ordinary phishing—the impersonation site echoed real balances and transactions because attackers held valid credentials that called the bank’s internal APIs and forwarded responses to the decoy portal.

Containment began by cutting edge communication and disabling the compromised professional account in Active Directory, which immediately stopped live data feeding the fake site. Investigation then mapped lateral use of that access, scoped indirect harm across more than fifteen financial brands, and pursued careful countermeasures on attacker infrastructure hosted on AWS. Rather than altering the adversary environment, the team preserved evidence while harvesting server data over several days, revealing a fraud-panel operation that could spin up branded phishing with CDN support in a handful of clicks. Parallel work covered malware tied to some targets, certificate and install-path differences, sandbox findings, and IOC sharing through MISP, plus coordination with institutions and authorities.

The closing material stresses SOC preparation—logging, asset priority, detection rules tuned for combined phishing-and-API abuse—and disciplined incident phases from identification through recovery. It also covers counterattack tradecraft such as masking investigator IPs, reading adversary logs for insight, and building multidisciplinary teams for incidents of this scale.

talks.title: How to Secure Your Software Supply Chain and Speed-Up DFIR with Hashlookup
talks.teaser: Shows how the hashlookup service identifies known software files to speed up forensic triage and supply chain checks.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from supply chain compromise, technique T1195, which kept appearing in threat intelligence shared through MISP. The speaker explains that the usual advice to verify distributed binaries by hash offers no easy route. Forensic analysts face huge file counts, poor coverage of modern Linux packages and containers, and awkward formats such as snaps, flatpaks and AppImages.

The team then presented hashlookup, an open project with a public service that works as a key-value store of file hashes. Its backend holds more than 25 billion keys from many distributions, including Ubuntu, Kali, CentOS and Fedora, plus JavaScript libraries from CDNJS. Each result shows how many parents have carried the same file, which acts as a rough trust signal. Weekly Bloom filter exports allow offline checks. The demo covered a MISP module, a graphical client, and a forensic analyzer script that can hash running processes from the proc filesystem.

The speaker argued that SBOMs usually omit full file hashes, so they are of limited use to investigators, and that organisations should baseline their own systems against known hashes. Vendors can be asked for per-release file hashes during procurement, and claims of zero dependencies deserve scrutiny. Planned work includes adding more publishers, splitting the Bloom filters by topic, and accepting hash submissions directly from software vendors.

talks.title: How to Talk to a Board so the Board Will Talk Back
talks.teaser: Shows security leaders how to build board trust and frame cyber risk in business terms directors can act on.
talks.summary:
Helen Patton opens with the core problem: security teams and boards do not share a language. Terms like risk mean different things to security and finance, and directors seldom have deep security experience. She argues that a board's job is to set strategic direction and ensure the organization is structured to follow it, not to review day-to-day controls.

The middle of the talk covers how to engage directors. Security leaders should check whether the board includes someone with real cyber risk expertise, how often they report, and whether they can reach directors directly. For new directors, she suggests onboarding that explains the business, its industry threats and what counts as normal, plus practical help such as multi-factor authentication for personal accounts. Inviting directors to tabletop exercises and sending pre-reads followed by one-on-one calls also help. For presentations, she recommends opening with a story, showing trends over time, framing risk around business lines, and using benchmarks carefully.

She closes with practical points: build personal trust with directors, because they need to know the report is truthful even when the news is unwelcome. Treat the people who manage board messaging as stakeholders, use vendors and cyber insurance contracts for exercises, decide ahead of time what is material enough to escalate, and describe outcomes rather than capabilities.

talks.title: Improving Sector Based Incident Response
talks.teaser: Presents a six-step framework for building sector incident response teams that fit into existing national cybersecurity structures.
talks.summary:
Justin Novak from the SEI presents a framework for building sector-based incident response teams, often called sector CERTs. He defines such a team as any body responsible for incident response within a subset of a country or economy, a deliberately broad definition meant to cover both mature and newly formed organizations. The case for these teams rests on threats designed for particular industries and on shared risk: when sector members pool information, each faces a smaller share of the total threat than it would alone.

The central problem is that a sector team sits in the middle of an existing national ecosystem of regional and national bodies, government agencies, other sector teams and constituents. Adding one disrupts established roles, funding and reporting lines, which can provoke resistance. The framework keeps that ecosystem at the center through six steps: satisfying prerequisites, gathering stakeholder input, evaluating gaps, building a roadmap, implementing, and reviewing afterward. Novak illustrates the prerequisite stage with service selection, so a new team does not duplicate what others already offer, and sketches two models: one where a national team triages reports and passes them down to sectors, and one led by the sector team and its members.

In the question session he said the post-implementation review feeds into a new development cycle, and acknowledged that the word responsible in his definition needed rewording. A listener noted that sector teams grown organically within their industries tended to have fewer trust problems than those a regulator tried to lead. For practitioners, the takeaway is to map stakeholders and existing services early, plan for disruption, and treat the framework as a repeating cycle rather than a one-time checklist.

talks.title: Incident Response Investigations in the Age of the Cloud
talks.teaser: A consultant walks through a cloud breach case and readiness moves for centralized logging and isolated response accounts.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with career context, then shifts to a real-world compromise dubbed nuclear orange: an IoT firmware startup lost proprietary code and AWS keys after repositories were made public. The victim relied on AWS, Windows AD, EKS managed by a third party, and Bitbucket-driven Jenkins in their build pipeline. Responders requested VPN, CloudTrail, Bitbucket, snapshot, S3, and VPC evidence, but SaaS log delivery arrived incomplete or filtered, many cloud logs were never enabled, and Kubernetes offered little forensic detail by default.

Analysis of CloudTrail tied activity to the Endgame AWS tooling via its default user agent. Untagged EKS snapshots forced manual reconstruction; a misconfigured Jenkins SSO let any Bitbucket user authenticate, and script-console abuse exposed credentials that enabled public S3 exfiltration. The speaker contrasts on-premises artifact richness with SaaS visibility gaps, retention limits, container ephemerality, and sampled network telemetry, while noting one-click centralization, snapshot automation, and native log agents as cloud advantages.

For practitioners, the closing guidance stresses a dedicated cloud IR account separate from the compromised tenant, templated analysis infrastructure for disks versus JSON logs, lightweight recurring log pulls where enterprise SIEM is unavailable, centralized logging without relying on vendor consoles, asset tagging, and least-privilege responder access to log buckets. A brief Q&A notes IAM denies and CloudTrail monitoring as secondary controls after credential theft from Jenkins.

talks.title: Internet Spelunking: IPv6 Scanning and Device Fingerprinting
talks.teaser: Shows how Shadowserver scans the internet over IPv4 and IPv6 and fingerprints exposed devices at scale.
talks.summary:
Shadowserver, a nonprofit that shares threat intelligence at no cost, explains how its internet scanning works and how it found new exposed services. Dave de Coster sets out the ground rules: scans use the smallest packets possible, are tested before they run, and avoid exploitation. The project began with DNS and other UDP protocols that were being abused for reflected DDoS, then moved on to TCP services. Today the team runs about 103 IPv4 scans and 10 IPv6 scans from 37 servers.

For IPv6, a full sweep is infeasible, so the team builds target lists from passive DNS, a public IPv6 hitlist, certificate transparency and partner sinkholes, covering about 814 million addresses in use. IPv6 probing is slower and starts losing packets at around 100,000 packets, compared with half a million on IPv4. The results showed that one in eight scanned IPv6 addresses answered HTTP, many with default pages, and that only 4% of IPv6 MySQL hosts had block lists, versus 40% on IPv4.

Piotr Kielczewski then described fingerprinting: a rule engine matches banners, certificate names, HTTP content and SNMP fields to identify device type, vendor, model and sector. About 1,200 rules currently classify devices from 173 vendors, up to 30 million devices daily. Examples include Roomba vacuums, Philips Hue systems and PLCs identified through non-native protocols. The takeaway is that exposed devices, not just open ports, reveal a country's risk, and CERTs can subscribe to this data for free.

talks.title: It's Just a Jump To The Left (of Boom)
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for It's Just a Jump To The Left (of Boom).

talks.title: Keynote: Cybersecurity's Image Problem and What We Can All Do About It
talks.teaser: Examines how fear-driven security messaging and imagery disempower the public, and which alternatives work better.
talks.summary:
Victoria Baines, a professor of IT at Gresham College and a former investigator with UK law enforcement and Europol, opens by arguing that cybersecurity communication is a form of persuasion. Drawing on classical rhetoric, she analyses how government agencies, security vendors and criminals address ordinary people about threats. Her close reading of national security strategy prefaces, consumer advertising, pandemic-era vendor messaging and criminal emails found that all three groups used similar techniques.

The main techniques were amplification, which exaggerates threats and urgency using statistics that are not backed by data, and the push to "click the thing" or buy a product to be safe. She showed the results of a cybercrime prevention image search, which were full of padlocks, blue light and a faceless hooded figure, and noted that an FBI page used the same kind of image until 2020. Consumer antivirus adverts cast viewers as intergalactic cyber warriors, and a vendor post that linked cyber threats to the pandemic was criticised for borrowing public health fear. Her concern is that such imagery makes people feel powerless and also sets unrealistic expectations for security staff, feeding burnout and recruitment problems.

As alternatives she pointed to the film Ralph Breaks the Internet, which presents online threats in an accessible way, to a UK reporting campaign for COVID-related scams that let members of the public take an active part, and to a public health model built on traditional hygiene campaigns. Her takeaway was to ask whether a message empowers people to protect themselves or simply scares them. In the Q&A she urged journalists to call a data breach a data breach rather than a hack.

talks.title: Keynote: Online Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM): The Insider Attack You Have Not Seen Coming
talks.teaser: Walks security teams through real CSAM incidents on their networks and the response lessons learned the hard way.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by outlining the forms of online child sexual exploitation, including grooming, live-streamed abuse, sextortion and the circulation of child sexual abuse material (CSAM). It points to rising volumes of reports to the US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children and argues that any platform or corporate network can be misused, including by its own staff, so the problem belongs to security teams.

Two incident case studies follow. In the first, a research and education organisation received a police notice about one of its IP addresses. Investigators traced it to a former employee who had gained access to a retired administrator's laptop and used it to share illegal files through a peer-to-peer client for about 30 days, a threat the mature security team had never modelled. In the second, an alert about uploads from an academic supercomputing centre led into a federated, multi-layer cloud platform. The operator had already deleted the affected virtual machines and logs, leaving investigators with only a few email addresses and IP addresses, and cross-border legal requests were slow.

The takeaways are practical. Treat this material as a cybercrime issue, load known hashes and indicators into existing detection tooling so analysts need not view images, and investigate hits instead of simply deleting them. Organisations should report to law enforcement, keep evidence forensically sound, shield staff from exposure including file names, and write CSAM-specific procedures covering incident response, HR and legal. Building a relationship with local police before an incident occurs is also advised.

talks.title: Keynote: What Do We Owe One Another In Cybersecurity?
talks.teaser: Argues that organizations in an interconnected ecosystem owe one another shared defense, especially smaller ones struggling to keep up.
talks.summary:
Wendy Nather opened the second day of the FIRST Cyber Threat Intelligence Symposium in Dublin by asking what organizations owe one another in security. She argued that businesses now operate as interconnected ecosystems, so a breach spreads well beyond its original target. Her main example was the Blackbaud ransomware incident, which affected more than a thousand organizations, many of them non-profits. A cited report found that more than one in four recipients of such ripple effects ended up paying all the costs despite not being breached.

The core of the talk concerned the security poverty line, the point below which smaller organizations cannot effectively protect themselves. Nather grouped the gap into money, expertise, capability and influence, and noted that vendors rarely publish prices, while estimates for a basic toolset could differ by a factor of four. Research she ran with the Scientia Institute linked a proactive technology refresh practice to better security outcomes, with modern, centralised infrastructure performing best. She then asked whether basic logging, single sign-on and incident response features should come at no extra charge, and whether large "linchpin" organizations should take on more responsibility.

In the question session, audience members compared security incident reporting with aviation safety and described medical research equipment that still runs Windows XP. Nather responded that such organizations should not simply be told to update. She closed by calling cooperation a civic and moral duty, and encouraged more voices from smaller organizations and more countries to share their challenges.

talks.title: Knowledge Management - Nourishing and Enhancing Your Communication and Intelligence
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Knowledge Management - Nourishing and Enhancing Your Communication and Intelligence.

talks.title: Living with Ransomware - The New Normal in Cyber Security
talks.teaser: Explains how ransomware gangs operate and shares real intrusion cases, plus practical detection, forensics and communication advice.
talks.summary:
Vishal Thakur, senior director of DFIR at Ankura's Australian practice, argues that ransomware is not going away and that organisations have to learn to live with it. He reviews the groups active today and the sectors they hit, including healthcare, supply chains, government and education. Motives range from money to disruption and testing new tooling. He notes a shift toward ransomware-as-a-service, which lowers the barrier for affiliates, and a move from encryption alone to extortion, where stolen data is threatened with publication even when backups exist.

He walks through two incidents. In the first, a freight company had been exposed since 2020, with attackers moving in and out for a long time, installing MEGAsync to exfiltrate data before encrypting everything. In the second, attackers used the ProxyLogon Exchange flaw, dropped tooling and spread through scheduled tasks, and lowered their ransom demand during negotiation. He stresses tabletop exercises, regular virtual machine snapshots, retained logs, and detection built from published threat intelligence and endpoint tools. Early engagement of incident responders is also recommended.

He closes with cyber insurance, whose costs have risen sharply and whose policies may cover response and negotiation help, and with communication. A single approved point of contact, consistent updates to customers and regulators, and control of the media narrative all matter for limiting brand damage. In questions, he confirmed that Linux servers and VMware ESXi hosts are being targeted, and that payment rates are hard to measure.

talks.title: More Than a CSIRT: Lessons Learned from Supporting a National Response to COVID-19
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in More Than a CSIRT: Lessons Learned from Supporting a National Response to COVID-19.

talks.title: Never Walk Alone: Inspirations From a Growing OWASP Project
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Never Walk Alone: Inspirations From a Growing OWASP Project.

talks.title: No More Ransomware in Critical Infrastructure!
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding No More Ransomware in Critical Infrastructure!.

talks.title: Open Source Doesn't Care About You, But You Should Care About It
talks.teaser: Explains why open source projects owe downstream users no support, and how suppliers and consumers can manage that risk.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that open source software owes its users nothing, so organizations that rely on it need to understand it and plan for that. The speaker sorts the people involved into personas: maintainers who write upstream code, suppliers who package it into products, and consumers who benefit from those products. He notes that much commercial software is built on open source components, and that many suppliers use projects without contributing back or knowing exactly what they ship.

He then describes how project maturity varies. Some projects are single-maintainer efforts with no formal security process, some are community projects with basic triage and documentation, and foundation-level projects such as kernel and Kubernetes have dedicated security teams and documented release timelines. Upstream support usually covers only the latest and previous versions, there are no service contracts, and contributors are often pseudonymous and spread across the world. The Log4j case shows the downstream effects: the embargo leaked, the Apache team shipped a patch within hours, the first fix was incomplete, a second fix followed days later, and two more CVEs surfaced. Some vendors were still shipping version 1, which had been deprecated years earlier.

The takeaways are to know every component you ship and where it came from, ask vendors how they handle upstream issues and notifications, and contribute back through patches, documentation, advisories, or funding. The speaker pointed to the OpenSSF ten-point mobilization plan, its working groups, and the Sigstore signing project as places to get involved.
