talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Prioritizing Vulnerability Response with a Stakeholder Specific Vulnerability Categorization.

talks.title: Ransomware Incident Response - The Real-World Story of a Ransomware Attack
talks.teaser: Traces a real ransomware intrusion from an exposed RDP login to domain compromise, and the recovery choices afterward.
talks.summary:
Joseph Carson walks through an incident response case involving the Crylock ransomware, a variant distributed through an affiliate program. The victim learned of the breach when the attackers contacted its security team directly, while they were still taking data. With logs cleared, the investigator traced the timestamps of remaining cleared event logs back to the first compromised machine, a database system used by an accountant. The business rebuilt from a one-year-old decommissioned server and hired staff to reconstruct about a year of lost records over roughly two to two and a half months, rather than paying the ransom.

The likely entry point was RDP brute force against that machine, which had been made publicly reachable at the accountant's request. Once inside, the attackers found a file of credentials on the desktop and used saved browser passwords. Their scripts disabled security tools in sessions shorter than Defender's auto-healing window, and they used Mimikatz to harvest credentials, added a backdoor user and set up a sticky keys backdoor. A backup script running PsExec under a domain administrator account gave them domain controller access, and ransomware was deployed about two hours later.

The main lessons are to practice incident response plans with finance, HR and other business teams instead of leaving them unused on file shares. Backups need protection from ransomware, including separate credentials. Least privilege, credential rotation and knowing when applications normally run help reveal misuse, such as activity on a weekend. Shadow IT created the exposure in this case, so it needs controlling.

talks.title: Ransomware, Risk, & Recovery: Protecting and Creating Resilience for Hybrid Active Directory
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Ransomware, Risk, & Recovery: Protecting and Creating Resilience for Hybrid Active Directory.

talks.title: Ransomware Stages of Grief
talks.teaser: Maps the stages of grief onto ransomware response, arguing that reaching acceptance early speeds recovery.
talks.summary:
Tony Curtly, director of incident command at Secureworks' incident response team, uses the Kubler-Ross stages of grief to describe how leaders react when ransomware hits. He opens with a scenario in which a manufacturing CIO learns that core systems are encrypted and millions of dollars are at stake each day. To show layered extortion, he plays a recorded voicemail from an actor who threatened to leak data to the press, staff and customers, taken from a real engagement.

Walking through each stage, he describes how denial drives rushed password resets and rebuilds that may need redoing if the attacker returns, and how anger shows up as blame. Depression can follow a root cause that points to a missed control, and bargaining pushes staff toward burnout. He suggests outside responders handle commodity rebuild work while internal staff cover application and business knowledge. One small company's IT director reached acceptance on day one and gave responders implicit trust, the fastest response he had seen. Other recoveries took one to four months, with one dominated by resetting 80,000 accounts.

Key takeaways include leaning on outside experts, avoiding price haggling, building a no-blame culture, and setting a 24-hour response tempo with rest. Preparation spans controls that stop attack steps and tested backups with known asset inventories. He closes by urging leaders to use the incident to improve the security environment at board level.

talks.title: Reversing Golang Binaries with Ghidra
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Reversing Golang Binaries with Ghidra.

talks.title: Rise of the Vermilion: Cross-platform Cobalt Strike Beacon Targeting Linux and Windows
talks.teaser: Traces a Cobalt Strike-style backdoor that targets both Linux and Windows, and why Linux variants go undetected.
talks.summary:
The talk examines Vermilion, a backdoor found in an ELF file that shared strings with Cobalt Strike, a commercial adversary simulation framework that is widely cracked and used by criminals. The speakers explain its components, including the team server, client, stager and beacon, and why its popularity makes attribution difficult. They also place it within a Linux threat landscape where coin miners and botnets are common.

The sample contained a high share of code the research team had never seen, suggesting it was written from scratch, and no vendor on VirusTotal flagged it. Its configuration used a simple single-byte cipher, and it fingerprinted hosts before sending encrypted, encoded data. Commands arrived mainly over DNS, with HTTP as an alternative, and covered browsing directories, transferring files and running commands. A Windows DLL pivoted from the command-and-control address, dating to 2019, had largely the same functionality. Working with McAfee Enterprise ATR, the team found the backdoor in live attacks on high-profile organisations, and assessed with high probability an advanced adversary, most likely a nation state, without naming one.

The closing discussion argued that Linux malware is overlooked because many users assume it needs little antivirus, and that embedded systems rarely run full endpoint tools. Practical takeaways included detecting the Windows payload in memory, hunting for the distinctive stager, reusing existing Cobalt Strike YARA signatures and network indicators, and recognising that sandboxing Linux samples is hard across distributions.

talks.title: Sightings Ecosystem: A Data-driven Analysis of ATT&CK in the Wild
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Sightings Ecosystem: A Data-driven Analysis of ATT&CK in the Wild.

talks.title: Speed is key: Leveraging the Cloud for Forensic Artifact Collection & Processing
talks.teaser: Outlines a cloud pipeline that pulls encrypted forensic triage from Windows endpoints via EDR and delivers analyst-ready results in minutes.
talks.summary:
The speakers frame incident response at a large global enterprise where intruders move quickly across hosts, full disk images take too long, and classic remote collection depends on end users running scripts across time zones and holidays. They argue that triage artifacts and actionable indicators matter more than enormous indicator lists, and that one-size enterprise forensic suites leave gaps across diverse cloud and platform estates.

They walk through a staged PowerShell workflow triggered through Microsoft Defender live response: a stager downloads the main collector, which gathers memory and CAPE-driven triage files, compresses and encrypts them with envelope encryption, and uploads to a write-only S3 bucket. Lambda replication preserves originals while EC2 workers decrypt, parse artifacts into CSVs, and enrich connections and browser data against internal ownership context. An HTTP API supplies case numbers, privacy-sensitive collection flags, and ordering tricks to beat console timeouts; a live demo uploads triage data in about ten minutes and memory later.

Practitioners gain a repeatable reference architecture emphasizing modularity, auditability for privacy counsel, and scale-out processing. Planned work includes open sourcing, infrastructure as code, more parsers, and tighter compliance automation by jurisdiction.

talks.title: Traffic Light Protocol 2022: Updates for An Improved Sharing Experience
talks.teaser: The session walks through FIRST TLP 2.0 revisions, sharing use cases for providers and victims, and the January 2023 adoption window.
talks.summary:
The panel opens with how Traffic Light Protocol grew from early UK sector sharing work into divergent national variants, and why US-CERT adoption friction led to a FIRST special interest group and TLP 1.0 in 2016. After years of quiet maintenance, a global consultation from 2019 produced TLP 2.0, approved by the FIRST board with over fifty contributors worldwide.

Version 2.0 keeps four colors but tightens plain-language rules, adds definitions for community, organization, and clients, and publishes a colors table with RGB, CMYK, and hex values plus accessibility tweaks. TLP:WHITE becomes TLP:CLEAR; TLP:AMBER retains version 1 meaning while TLP:AMBER+STRICT limits sharing to the organization only. Speakers illustrate day-to-day problems: outsourcing and incident-response firms, re-marking when amber would over-travel, victim notifications that separate envelope restrictions from payload sensitivity, cheat sheets, and paragraph or tear-line markings in one message.

Publication follows the symposium with a transition window until 1 January 2023 so tools, firmware, and habits can adjust, especially where TLP:WHITE was hard-coded. Practitioners should treat TLP as a sharing label, not action policy, talk to originators when labels are unclear, and feed real use cases back to the SIG for ongoing guidance and translations.

talks.title: The Blue Side of Documentation
talks.teaser: Offers practical guidance for SOC analysts on structuring documentation, avoiding bloat, and keeping hunting queries at hand.
talks.summary:
The presentation addresses a common SOC problem: documentation exists in scattered wiki pages, yet analysts cannot find or trust it. The speaker describes joining a European security company where Confluence held unused text, then imposing structure by gathering pages, cutting deprecated content, and aligning docs with two priorities—onboarding new analysts and describing the alert-handling lifecycle.

Operational tactics include assigning a point of contact per topic, running a full-day team documentation event, and shifting from long explanatory prose toward copy-paste hunting queries for Azure, MDE, Elastic, and XDR stacks. Polarity supplements the wiki with investigator-oriented annotations, OCR on screenshots, and short notes on living-off-the-land binaries so junior staff get context beside live alerts. Alert-specific pages pair brief handling rationale with ready-made queries to shorten time-to-triage.

Closing guidance stresses iterative scope: plan but do not freeze the knowledge base, write only what people will reuse, revisit every three to four months, and document for present needs rather than hypothetical futures. The speaker sketches a move toward Markdown in Obsidian, backlinks, GitHub versioning, and cross-linking offensive team write-ups so defensive readers can pivot quickly.

talks.title: There is No TTP
talks.teaser: Examines why MITRE ATT&CK tactics, techniques, and procedures are often misapplied in detection, attribution, and automation.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens with the claim that defenders cannot detect “TTPs” as a bundle because the label mixes three different ideas that must be separated to be useful. He traces his path from a junior threat analyst in 2014 through Ryan Stilians’s blog posts and later heavy use of MITRE ATT&CK, paired with a show-of-hands survey and a Matrix-themed contrast between common community assumptions and his view after reading ATT&CK’s design and philosophy paper.

For each layer he alternates “blue pill” community impressions with “red pill” critiques and short incident-driven examples. Tactical rows in ATT&CK are framed as objectives or kill-chain phases, not deployable behaviors comparable to military tactics such as ambush; he cites stealth shifting to smash-and-grab or scorched-earth behavior after detection as patterns responders could catalog. Techniques aid heat maps and coverage conversations but are too coarse for attribution; detections target implementations and traces, not abstract technique IDs. He describes building the open source Adversary Emulation Planner by modeling technique dependencies until behavior versus outcome definitions broke automation workflows.

On procedures, he notes procedure examples live in prose while the object model offers technique IDs without procedure IDs, illustrated through Mimikatz versus OS credential dumping reporting and information loss. He closes with a personal roadmap: retire misleading “what you get” techniques, enumerate real tactics and machine-readable procedures, and explore STIX-style patterning for analytics, pointing listeners to the Socrates SOC automation research effort.

talks.title: Threats versus Capabilities Building Better Detect and Respond Capabilities
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Threats versus Capabilities Building Better Detect and Respond Capabilities.

talks.title: The SolarWinds Supply Chain Compromise
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for The SolarWinds Supply Chain Compromise.

talks.title: Timing is Everything: Generic Trigger Events for Malware Memory Dumping
talks.teaser: Shows generic memory-dump trigger events that capture unpacked malware payloads across many families, with reduced maintenance.
talks.summary:
Matthias and Patrick, who both do malware analysis and reverse engineering at VMware, explain why malware is often shipped packed or encrypted to slip past scanners. Writing a separate unpacker for every packer is complex and needs constant upkeep, so they look at memory dumping instead: run the sample, let it unpack itself, then dump the payload from process memory at the right moment. The hard parts are timing and performance, because pausing execution to copy memory slows everything down, and dumping too often floods the analyst with noise.

They review existing approaches. Dumping executable regions when a process terminates is simple and still useful, but the data can be gone by then. Dumping regions as they are freed or overwritten gives far more dumps, many of them irrelevant when frameworks reuse memory. The PE-sieve library uses heuristics to detect injected payloads, while CAPE uses debugger rules that need prior knowledge of each family and break when a family changes. The speakers then present a small set of generic triggers. The first network behavior trigger dumps executable and writable regions and thread stacks once a sample first connects out. Other triggers cover .NET reflective loading, content changes in watched regions, and signature scans run only on events such as memory being freed. Dumps are prioritised, size-limited and capped by a global quota.

Their collection results show that first network behavior alone caught 46% of Agent Tesla payloads, rising past 70% with the content change trigger. For Emotet it covered 84% of samples, and 99% when first execution was added. LuckyBot reached 76% on first network behavior, and NanoCore passed 90% with the rules applied. The takeaway is that a few family-independent triggers can cover many malware families with far less maintenance than family-specific unpackers.

talks.title: VEXed by Vulnerabilities That Don't Affect Your Product? Try This!
talks.teaser: Explains how VEX statements let vendors and customers flag which vulnerabilities truly affect a product, using CSAF and SBOM data.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at what security teams do when a headline vulnerability, such as Log4j, lands and they must work out which of their products are exposed and where reliable answers can be found. The presenters point to rising vulnerability counts, the extra visibility that software bill of materials bring, and scanner false positives as reasons that manual investigation does not scale.

The core proposal is VEX, a machine-readable statement that a product is not affected by a given vulnerability, or that it is fixed or under investigation. The presenters explain that VEX is a profile of the Common Security Advisory Framework, so it reuses the same format, distribution and tooling. Each document names products through a product tree that can be matched against an asset database or an SBOM, then gives a status backed by either an impact statement or an action statement. For not-affected claims they outlined five machine-readable justifications, including that the component is not present, that the vulnerable code is not present, that an attacker cannot control the code, that the code is not in the execution path, and that an inline mitigation exists elsewhere. They also showed short JSON examples and noted how SBOM components can be linked in CycloneDX and SPDX.

Open problems include the effort vendors face in building product trees, the lack of stable unique product identifiers, and the trust questions around pushed versus pulled distribution. The practical takeaway is to ask vendors for VEX documents and to clean up asset inventories so that incoming advisories have something to match against.

talks.title: Watching Webpages in Action with Lookyloo
talks.teaser: Explains how Lookyloo records and maps everything a webpage loads, to expose phishing redirects and hidden trackers.
talks.summary:
Lookyloo is a forensic tool from CIRCL for examining what a web page does when it loads. Instead of using an analyst's everyday browser, it runs the page in a dedicated headless browser, records every request and resource, and draws them as a tree arranged over time. Each resource is hashed and kept locally, so the same stylesheet or script can be matched across many captures. The idea came from a 2015 meeting with media lawyers who wanted to know what was on their own sites.

The examples ranged widely. The EFF homepage loaded six scripts, three stylesheets and twenty images, while the Fox News front page produced a tree so large that the code had to be reworked to cope. Phishing cases included a fake crypto wallet site and a fake Luxembourg government login, where redirects hid the real infrastructure and a shared stylesheet linked the pages to others. The speakers also showed GDPR problems, such as the Mirror newspaper loading Google and DoubleClick content in an iframe, with cookies set before consent.

The tool supports custom user agents, cookies, referrers, proxies and geolocation, and integrates with VirusTotal, urlscan.io and MISP through an API. The presenters warned against using their browser extension with a public instance, since login cookies could be uploaded. Their advice was to run a private instance and keep captures in-house. Planned work includes passive SSL lookups, Pandora file analysis and a UI revamp.

talks.title: Who Do You Think You Are?
talks.teaser: Maps evolving CTI standards and sharing organizations from CVE and IoDEF through STIX/TAXII to voluntary and mandatory reporting.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames cyber threat intelligence as a family tree: standards and sharing bodies that branched, competed, and converged over decades, with an oral-history spirit rather than a precise chronology. Starting from MITRE ATT&CK as a contemporary leaf—without dwelling on ATT&CK itself—the talk walks backward through CVE, early incident-exchange work, IoDEF and related efforts, OpenIOC, DOTS, and coordination attempts to unify diverse formats. It recounts why IoDEF saw uneven uptake, liability worries around “incident” in the name, and how STIX and TAXII emerged from U.S. federal sharing needs, including anecdotal naming and the path through OASIS, plus CyBOX integration and TLP’s UK roots.

On the organization side, the narrative moves from the 1988 CERT response after the Morris worm and FIRST’s geographic rationale, through InfraGard, presidential direction on critical infrastructure, the growth of sector ISACs and later ISAOs, and mechanisms such as CISA-related protections and various U.S. public–private portals. UK examples cover CPNI, NCSC consolidation of former sharing roles, and voluntary industry partnerships contrasted with regulated reporting routes.

The close examines a shift from voluntary coalitions toward mandatory incident notification—defense supply chains, NIS-style rules, and New York financial licensing—and how duplicate reporting obligations may crowd voluntary channels. The speaker seeks audience contributions to fill gaps in the tree; Q&A reinforces that standards keep evolving, that automation may favor newer exchange models, and that pre-IoDEF statistical exchange work deserves a place in the lineage.
